title: The 1.5°C target will be missed. Where does climate action go from here?
gist: Chatham House argues the 1.5°C Paris limit will be overshot (current policies imply ~2.7°C by 2100), turning climate impacts systemic — hitting supply chains, insurability and financial stability — and pushing policy toward adaptation. It warns adaptation demand could derail mitigation (already visible in European politics) and proposes a three-criteria merit order (protection, mitigation-compatibility, public confidence), using air conditioning vs heat pumps as the test case.

insights.claim: Chatham House says overshooting the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C warming limit is now effectively locked in, with the UN assessing the overshoot as 'widely assessed as unavoidable' only a decade after Paris was signed.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Climate-risk models and portfolios pinned to 1.5°C pathways need re-basing to overshoot scenarios.
insights.quote: Overshooting the 1.5°C target is ‘widely assessed as unavoidable’, according to the UN
insights.locator: Only a decade after governments signed

insights.claim: Under current policies global warming is expected to reach 2.7°C by 2100, putting even the Paris Agreement's 'well below 2°C' aim in jeopardy, per Chatham House.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Long-dated physical-risk stress tests should use ~2.7°C+ as a central case rather than a tail.
insights.quote: under current policies 2.7°C is expected by the end of the century
insights.locator: Only a decade after governments signed

insights.claim: COP31 president Murat Kurum warned that even a brief overshoot of 1.5°C would cause irreversible loss and damage and that overshoot extent and duration must be minimized.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals COP policy framing shifting from 'avoid 1.5°C' to 'minimize overshoot duration', relevant for carbon removal and mitigation policy demand.
insights.quote: even a brief overshoot would cause ‘irreversible loss and damage’

insights.claim: Chatham House argues that breaching 1.5°C will shift climate impacts from discrete, local extreme-weather events hitting farm regions and cities to systemic, global episodes that disrupt supply chains and unsettle financial stability.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect climate shocks to transmit through supply chains and financial systems, not just local asset damage — widen correlation assumptions.
insights.quote: They will go from discrete and local extreme weather events that hit agricultural regions and cities, to systemic and global episodes that hit supply chains and unsettle financial stability.

insights.claim: Chatham House notes 2026 extreme weather events — European heatwaves and catastrophic flooding in Nepal — in some cases exceeded what climate models had predicted.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Model-based physical-risk estimates may be systematically understated; haircut reliance on them.
insights.quote: In some cases, they have been beyond even what climate models have predicted
insights.locator: This year has seen many extreme

insights.claim: A group of senior insurance-industry whistleblowers has warned that insurers are increasingly struggling to insure assets, including homes, because of climate risk, raising doubts about the viability of the industry's operating model; Chatham House says overshoot will escalate this.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch P&C insurer underwriting retreat, rising premiums and uninsurable property zones as a channel into mortgage and real-estate valuations.
insights.quote: the insurance industry is increasingly struggling to insure assets – including homes – due to climate risk and raised concerns about the viability of its operating model

insights.claim: Climate policy discourse is pivoting toward adaptation — once dismissed as a concern for vulnerable nations, a distraction from emissions cuts or a form of defeatism — because climate impacts have accelerated faster than expected.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Adaptation spending (flood defences, cooling, resilience infrastructure) is becoming a mainstream policy and capex theme in rich countries.
insights.quote: the speed at which climate impacts have progressed has changed the tone and focused minds

insights.claim: The EU's climate chief has declared Europe must prepare for 3°C of warming by 2100, and the European Commission has built a framework for managing climate risk at the scale of entire social and economic systems.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: EU-level planning around 3°C implies regulatory push for systemic climate-risk management, likely flowing into financial supervision and infrastructure standards.
insights.quote: Europe must prepare for 3°C of warming by 2100
insights.locator: Stark public warnings are now being issued

insights.claim: The UK government has framed climate and nature loss as a top-tier national security threat (per Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband), set up a resilience taskforce and appointed the world's first climate-security envoy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Securitization of climate in the UK could unlock defence/resilience-style budgets for adaptation.
insights.quote: the climate crisis and nature loss are a national security threat of the highest order
insights.locator: Stark public warnings are now being issued

insights.claim: Despite rising awareness, Chatham House sees a widening gap between adaptation needs and the scale of adaptation investment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: An under-funded adaptation gap points to future public spending and private capital opportunities in resilience.
insights.quote: there is a growing gap between adaptation needs and the scale of investment

insights.claim: Chatham House warns that rising demand for protection from climate hazards can push governments into piecemeal 'band-aid' adaptation that worsens emissions or creates new vulnerabilities — e.g. coastal flood defences that caused biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation and higher flood risk in neighbouring coastal regions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Maladaptive infrastructure can shift rather than reduce risk — scrutinize adaptation projects for spillover effects on adjacent assets.
insights.quote: piecemeal, band-aid solutions to emerging threats
insights.locator: The growing focus on adaptation is not without risk

insights.claim: The greater danger, per Chatham House, is that as people experience climate impacts, demands for protection divert resources and attention away from mitigation, derailing emissions-reduction progress.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A political pivot from mitigation to adaptation is a downside risk for decarbonization-policy-dependent sectors (renewables, carbon markets).
insights.locator: An even greater danger might be

insights.claim: Early signs of the derailment dynamic are visible in Europe: the 2024 Valencia floods boosted climate-denying politicians, and after the UK's hottest summer on record Reform Party politicians argued for prioritizing heat adaptation over mitigation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Climate disasters may paradoxically strengthen anti-mitigation parties — a political risk for net-zero policy durability in Europe.
insights.quote: a climate-driven disaster boosted climate-denying politicians

insights.claim: Chatham House argues climate politics will shift quickly above 1.5°C from mitigating a future problem to demanding responses to deadly consequences today, and without preparation this could become a major problem for mitigation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect abrupt policy-priority swings after major climate disasters; position for volatility in climate-policy-exposed assets.
insights.locator: Doing this will require politicians to anticipate

insights.claim: Chatham House contends mitigation becomes more urgent, not less, after 1.5°C is breached because each fraction of a degree brings environmental tipping points closer, and prioritizing adaptation over mitigation perpetuates the need for adaptation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Counters the '1.5°C is lost so mitigation is moot' narrative; supports continued policy backing for decarbonization.
insights.quote: Focusing on adapting to climate risk at the expense of mitigating further warming risks perpetuating the conditions which create the need for adaptation in the first place.

insights.claim: Chatham House proposes that adaptation investments meet three criteria: maximize protection today and in future (robust across scenarios), complement rather than undermine mitigation, and command public confidence in their protective value.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A usable screen for which resilience technologies are likely to win policy support and subsidies.
insights.locator: Thirdly – to help with the above point

insights.claim: Under Chatham House's framework, air conditioning not powered by renewables protects people and is trusted but works against mitigation, while heat pumps (heating in winter, cooling in summer) protect and complement mitigation but lack public confidence in Britain as heat-protection measures.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Heat pumps could capture adaptation demand for cooling if the public narrative shifts — a demand catalyst to watch for heat-pump makers in the UK.
insights.quote: Air conditioning (if not powered by renewables) meets the first and third criteria but not the second.

insights.claim: Chatham House says no one has yet systematically ranked adaptation options against all three criteria, and doing so would create a new 'merit order' of adaptation options and reveal work still needed, such as changing the narrative on heat pumps.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A future adaptation merit order could steer public funding toward dual-use (adaptation + mitigation) technologies.
insights.quote: it would help create a new merit order of options

insights.claim: Chatham House concludes an integrated approach to mitigation and adaptation is the key to navigating 1.5°C overshoot, with governments prioritizing protection and closing adaptation investment gaps while making clear, consistent commitments to accelerate mitigation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Favors policies and assets that serve both goals simultaneously (renewable-powered cooling, heat pumps, nature-positive defences).
insights.quote: An integrated approach to mitigation and adaptation is the key to navigating 1.5°C overshoot.
